Its constant-output alternative handles functions requiring no query, including an empty coordinate register. The finite-model results establish that the displayed infimum is an attained budget.
QuarticQuery.QLe: An admissible budget allows either a constant answer on the promise or a finite workspace, unit starting vector, and adaptive program with the stated cap and success at least $2/3$. All existential choices precede `∀ x b`, so the algorithm is uniform over inputs. The constant alternative handles empty coordinate sets, whose indexed query space has no unit vector. Off-promise inputs are exempt from correctness but remain covered by the syntactic cap.
QuarticQuery.Q_le_D: Every partial Boolean function on finitely many coordinates satisfies $Q(f)\leq D(f)$. A deterministic tree can be realized as a finite adaptive quantum program with the same cap, and exact correctness implies success at least $2/3$. The explicit constant alternative handles empty coordinate types. This comparison establishes nonemptiness of quantum admissible budgets and does not assume a randomized-to-quantum simulation theorem.
QuarticQuery.Q_le_iff: The numerical inequality $Q(f)\leq q$ holds exactly when `QLe f q` holds. The equivalence uses existence of a read-all algorithm and monotonicity of the admissible budgets. It therefore lets a proof move between an attained optimal query number and a concrete state-and-program witness, including the constant-answer alternative. All correctness remains uniform over the entire promise.
QuarticQuery.Q_reindex: A coordinate bijection preserves quantum complexity exactly. The construction transports the query-register basis, conjugates the fixed gates and projectors, and moves the initial state through the corresponding isometry. Every output mass and syntactic cap is preserved for the renamed input. Applying the inverse bijection gives the opposite inequality. This justifies replacing structured finite coordinates by a numbered finite set.
QuarticQuery.QueryTree: A deterministic algorithm whose internal nodes query one input coordinate and branch on its Boolean answer. A leaf returns a Boolean result. The constructor `.query i onFalse onTrue` fixes the queried coordinate at that node; later choices can depend on earlier answers through the branch taken. Depth counts the longest path and charges repeated queries as well.
QuarticQuery.QueryTree.depth: A leaf has depth zero, and a query node has one plus the larger depth of its children. This maximum includes every branch in the syntax, even one inconsistent with earlier answers or outside the promise. Repeated queries are therefore charged again. Depth is independent of the input and gives a uniform cap on every evaluation path; simplifying inconsistent branches is a separate convention argument.
QuarticQuery.QueryTree.eval: Evaluation returns a leaf’s stored answer or recursively follows the child selected by the queried input bit. Lean’s query constructor stores the false child before the true child, while the conditional checks the true case first. The tree and its queried coordinates are fixed syntactically; only the path depends on the input. Evaluation is defined even on inputs outside a later promise.
QuarticQuery.R: The least query budget for a randomized algorithm that returns the right answer with probability at least $2/3$ on every promised input. `RLe f t` describes one algorithm whose maximum tree depth is at most $t$; it is not an average query cost. The coordinate type is finite. For a total Boolean function, `totalise` makes every input promised.
QuarticQuery.RLe: `RLe f budget` requires one finite positive mixture of trees with depth at most `budget` and success at least $2/3$ at every defined input. The success threshold is inclusive. The mixture is chosen before the universal input and label quantifiers, and its depth is a maximum over all supported trees. Undefined inputs have no success requirement, but they do not change the program’s cap.
QuarticQuery.R_le_D: A randomized algorithm can use a deterministic tree with probability one, so $R(f)\leq D(f)$ for every partial Boolean function on finitely many coordinates. The deterministic tree must be correct everywhere on the promise, which is stronger than randomized success at least $2/3$. Both use a maximum query count over branches, including off-promise executions. This comparison does not require the function to be total.
QuarticQuery.R_le_iff: The inequality $R(f)\leq q$ holds exactly when there is a randomized program satisfying `RLe f q`. This connects a numerical lower or upper bound to the algorithmic predicate. It depends on the read-all witness and monotonicity of admissible budgets, so the natural infimum behaves as an attained minimum. The function may be partial, and correctness is still required only on its promise.
QuarticQuery.R_reindex: A bijection of finite coordinate types leaves randomized query complexity unchanged. Relabeling every query node preserves its tree depth and transports its evaluation, so the same fixed mixture works on the renamed promise. Applying the inverse bijection gives equality rather than only one inequality. The theorem uses `reindex e f`, which also transports undefined inputs correctly.
QuarticQuery.RandomizedProgram: A randomized algorithm represented by finitely many deterministic query trees with positive weights summing to one. The weights and trees are fixed before the input; randomness chooses which tree runs. `weight_pos` excludes zero-weight support entries. The maximum depth of these supported trees is the query cost. The finite-model appendix explains how distributions over bounded trees reduce to this representation.
QuarticQuery.RandomizedProgram.depth: A randomized program’s depth is the finite maximum of the depths of its component trees. Since every stored weight is positive, this is the maximum over its actual support. A very unlikely tree is charged just as fully as a likely one. The definition therefore measures an all-branch query cap, not the average number of queries under the random choice.
QuarticQuery.RandomizedProgram.success: For a fixed input $x$ and requested answer $b$, success is the sum of the weights of trees whose evaluation returns $b$. The definition works for either label and for every input, without referring to a promise. Correctness for a partial function is imposed later by substituting its defined label. Summing the two output masses gives one because each tree returns exactly one Boolean answer.
QuarticQuery.SemanticReview.orMixture: This randomized program on two input bits has three trees, each with weight $1/3$: output true immediately, read the first bit, or read the second bit. The choice is fixed before seeing the input, and its maximum depth is one. The positive real weights are part of the model; implementing exactly one third is not the same as sampling with a fixed finite number of fair coin flips.
QuarticQuery.SemanticReview.orMixture_su: On input $11$, all three trees return the correct OR value and success is one. On each other two-bit input, exactly two of the three equally weighted trees are correct, so success is $2/3$. The theorem gives this entire success law as one conditional expression. It demonstrates why the inclusive threshold in `RLe` matters, but does not by itself prove optimality among all one-query mixtures.
QuarticQuery.SemanticReview.orTwo_R_eq_o: The randomized complexity of total two-bit OR is exactly one. The three-tree mixture supplies success at least $2/3$ with cap one, and the presence of both output labels rules out zero queries. This is an all-branch cap in the arbitrary-real-mixture model. The declaration does not state the deterministic value two or the quantum value one; those require separate arguments.
QuarticQuery.SemanticReview.trueOnly: The one-bit partial function returns `some true` when its input bit is true and `none` when it is false. It therefore prescribes no answer at zero. A constant-true program is correct on the whole promise with zero queries. Replacing `none` by `some false` would create the total identity function, so undefined inputs must not be filled with false during model comparisons.
QuarticQuery.SemanticReview.trueOnly_Q_e: The same one-sided one-bit promise has quantum complexity zero through the explicit constant-answer alternative in `QLe`. No query register, initial quantum state, or measurement is needed to return true on all promised inputs. The declaration concerns this partial function, not the total identity obtained by assigning false to the undefined input. Its cost is zero on every branch, including off-promise executions.
QuarticQuery.SemanticReview.trueOnly_R_e: The partial one-bit function defined only at the true input has randomized complexity zero. A mixture concentrated on the constant-true tree already succeeds with probability one at every promised input, so no input query is needed. The false input remains outside the promise. This example illustrates that extending a partial function’s domain can increase complexity even when the old prescribed value stays unchanged.
QuarticQuery.TestIndex: The fixed set of local-test labels contains one label for each column bit, one for each other column, and one for each gate and each of two outputs in every transcript. `Fin S ⊕ Bool` distinguishes the $S$ gate-consistency tests from the two additional output tests. The labels do not depend on the candidate column or its proposed address.
QuarticQuery.Tournament.IsComparison: A comparison table in which the two orientations of every distinct pair sum to one and no candidate beats itself. The structure has two fields, `complementary` and `self_zero`; it does not itself assert that entries lie between zero and one. The companion predicate `UnitValued` supplies those bounds. Neither definition assumes an ordering or transitivity.
QuarticQuery.Tournament.UnitValued: Every entry $a_{ij}$ lies in $[0,1]$. This condition makes the entries usable as probabilities and ensures that multiplying a candidate's weight by one of them cannot increase its weight. It is separate from complementarity and the zero diagonal. The actual circuit construction obtains these bounds from a normalized output law rather than assuming that arbitrary real entries are probabilities.
QuarticQuery.Tournament.expected_final_w: Starting from unit weights, the expected total remaining weight after $T$ ideal rounds is at most $m/2^T$. The hypotheses `hc` and `ha` provide complementary comparisons and entries in $[0,1]$. The expectation includes histories at which all weights become zero; such a history remains at zero. No dominant candidate is needed for this decay estimate.
QuarticQuery.Tournament.expected_weight_: For positive total weight $W$, the weighted average of the next total weight is at most $W/2$. The hypotheses are complementarity, a zero diagonal, and `hW` identifying $W$ with the sum of current weights. The algebra subtracts a sum of squares. Nonnegative weights are needed for its probabilistic interpretation, and the zero-weight absorbing case is handled separately in the iterative argument.
QuarticQuery.Tournament.ideal_miss_le: The probability that $s$ is absent from the ideal list is at most the probability that remaining weight is at least $1/2$, which is at most $2m/2^T$. The hypotheses specify a complementary probability table, dominance, and $T\varepsilon<1/2$. Absence forces the dominant weight to remain large. The declaration exposes the two event bounds; the intermediate expectation is used inside the proof.
QuarticQuery.Tournament.weight: Each candidate starts with weight one. Adding pivot $p$ multiplies candidate $i$'s current weight by $a_{ip}$. Lean stores the newest pivot at the head of a list, so the recursive definition reads the older list first. These weights are quantities used to analyze the algorithm; the algorithm need not compute or estimate them.
QuarticQuery.UniversalPower: A nonnegative exponent $\alpha$ for which there is a positive constant $C$ satisfying $R(f)\le C(1+Q(f))^\alpha$ for every total Boolean function on every nonempty finite bit string. The constant is chosen before $n$ and $f$. `totalise f` embeds a total function into the partial-function query model without excluding any input.
QuarticQuery.Upper.Fkm_QLe: For `hk : 1 ≤ k`, `ht : 1 ≤ t`, and a circuit satisfying `hC : CircuitRealises C (P k t)`, the constructed total Boolean function has an error-$1/3$ quantum algorithm within `budget`. The chosen repetition count `n` must be at least the prescribed count, as stated by `hn`. The theorem applies to every realizing circuit, before substituting the size estimate for the particular Forrelation circuit.
QuarticQuery.Upper.Fkm_forrCircuit_QLe: For $k=l+1$ and $t\ge1$, one quantum program evaluates the total function from the named circuit with success at least $2/3$ and a global cap $C_k2^t(2t)^6$. The conclusion is `QLe`, which includes a witness program and its syntactic branch bound. It therefore expresses the all-input budget directly. Taking the minimum over programs gives the separate numerical inequality for $Q$.
QuarticQuery.Upper.IsCirc.symm: If a finite coherent isometry has an implementation with $n$ logical reads, its inverse also has an implementation with $n$ logical reads. The hypothesis `hF : IsCirc n F` supplies the original circuit. Reverse the gate order, invert each input-independent gate, and reuse the self-inverse reads. This proves access to the inverse preparation while keeping all workspace. Compiling either direction with the conservative physical compiler costs at most $2n$ bit queries.
QuarticQuery.Upper.Q_Fkm_le: For the explicit Forrelation circuit with $k=l+1$ and $t\ge1$, the total function has quantum query complexity at most $C_k2^t(2t)^6$. Using $m=4^t$, this is $C_k\sqrt m(\log_2m)^6$. The budget counts physical bit queries in the stated model. The circuit is the same named circuit used in the fixed-parameter classical family, rather than an unrelated existential witness.
QuarticQuery.Upper.Q_Fkm_le_exponential: For $t\ge1$ and $k=l+1\ge1$, the particular total function built with `forrCircuit` has quantum cost at most $2^{53}k2^{10k}2^t(2t)^6$. The bound is valid when $k$ varies; no constant depending on $k$ is hidden. The circuit is fixed in the function named by the conclusion. This does not itself prove the subsequent growing-family exponent comparison.
QuarticQuery.Upper.addrCost: `addrCost k t n` is $40t\,nk$: there are $40t$ address bits, each uses $n$ repetitions, and each repetition uses $k$ logical reads. In the paper’s notation $r=40t$ and $n=q$. This definition counts logical reads before the conservative factor of two for physical compilation. It is a cost expression; successful decoding also needs the repetition-error and promise hypotheses.
QuarticQuery.Upper.ampLaw: `ampLaw f q` assigns mass $f$ to failure and mass $(1-f)q_b/\sum_cq_c$ to successful label $b$. The definition alone is not a probability theorem: nonnegative weights, a suitable failure probability, and the zero-total case must be checked separately. In the tournament, $q_b$ is proportional to the current weight of candidate $b$, so the normalization cancels the common preparation factor.
QuarticQuery.Upper.budget: The integer budget adds $T$ padded tournament stages and $T$ fresh candidate verifications. Each verifier pays twice the logical address-decoding cost plus the physical failing-test search cost. The stage and search definitions already include trial counts, iteration counts, and the factor of two per logical read. Consequently this is a maximum physical input-query budget, not an expected cost or a preparation-call count.
QuarticQuery.Upper.budgetConst: The definition sets $R=1+1920000\,2^{10k}$, $C_c=40Rk+4$, and $C_K=42+20C_F(k)$, then combines the tournament and verifier coefficients as $6(48002\cdot258C_c)+6(40Rk+48002\cdot69C_K)$. The inputs contain only $k$, so the constant is independent of $t$. It is deliberately generous and records the paper’s padded physical-query accounting rather than an optimized leading constant.
QuarticQuery.Upper.budgetConst_eq_expand: The existing algorithm’s budget constant equals the displayed sum of one exponential term and two polynomial terms in $k$. Lean’s `budgetConst k` is defined from the previously chosen repetition and search costs; this theorem expands those definitions by arithmetic. It does not count a new algorithm. The exact expression is useful only because the next bound controls its dependence on a growing $k$.
QuarticQuery.Upper.budgetConst_le_expone: For $k\ge1$, the quantum-budget constant is at most $2^{53}k2^{10k}$. The assumption `hk` supplies that range. The proof expands the existing constant and absorbs the polynomial terms using $k\le2^{10k}$. This isolates how increasing the Forrelation order affects the same algorithm, which is needed when balancing the loss in the classical exponent.
QuarticQuery.Upper.budget_le: The hypothesis `hSz` bounds circuit size by `forrConstant k * mValue t * (2*t)^2`, and `ht` requires $t\geq1$. Under these assumptions, the exact budget using the prescribed decoder repetitions and actual test count is at most $C_k2^t(2t)^6$. This is arithmetic about the budget; it does not assume that the circuit realizes the promise problem. Correctness for a realizing circuit is supplied separately by `Fkm_QLe`.
QuarticQuery.Upper.cmpCost: The logical-read cost of one comparison is twice the address cost plus two pointer checks of depth $2t+1$. Lean groups the additions as `addrCost + (addrCost + ((2*t+1)+(2*t+1)))`, which is the paper’s $2a+2(2t+1)$. This includes both candidate addresses even when a particular branch could terminate sooner. The same padded bound applies to every input.
QuarticQuery.Upper.decode_samples: For $k\ge1$, any placement of the auxiliary input coordinates and any number $n$ of trials, a finite coherent preparation has the Boolean law `bern (decodeProb k t n z)` and uses $nk$ logical reads. `decodeProb` is the binomial tail at $n\delta^2/2$. `Samples` retains a unitary preparation and its workspace. The logical count is not, by itself, a statement that this many physical bit-oracle calls suffice.
QuarticQuery.Upper.le_vall_of_mem: If candidate $s$ occurs in $L$, sequential verification accepts with probability at least $v(s)$. The premise `h` bounds every verifier probability between zero and one, and `hs` states list membership. Earlier successful verifications can only help the event that someone accepts. The conclusion does not require $s$ to be dominant or to have a particularly large verification probability.
QuarticQuery.Upper.slice_opaqueSlot: On an index slice satisfying the control predicate `P`, the fixed slot applies one Grover step; on a false slice it is the identity. The preparation `U` and its inverse are applied unconditionally, and only the known reflections depend on the control. The result holds for arbitrary superposed input vector `ψ`. Here `S` specifies a success subset of basis labels and `o` is a basis origin.
QuarticQuery.Upper.testCost: The common local-test read budget is $\max\{3,2t+1\}$. The constant three covers the circuit-consistency tests, while $2t+1$ covers a pointer’s $2t$ address bits and one target bit. Using the maximum gives one cap for the controlled family of all tests. Physical compilation and amplification multiply this logical-read count later; they are not included in `testCost`.
QuarticQuery.Upper.testLaw: The law chooses a local-test index uniformly and returns that index if its exact test fails; otherwise it returns `none`. Each index contributes mass $1/K$, where $K$ is the number of tests. Thus the total successful-label mass is the fraction of failing tests. Here “success” means finding a defect, so `none` corresponds to accepting the proposed certificate only after the later amplification search has failed to find one.
QuarticQuery.Upper.tournament_runs: For at least two candidates, uniformly realizable comparison samplers and verifier programs produce one bounded Boolean program. The comparison assumptions are `hc`, `hu`, and `hcmp`; `hv` realizes each fresh verifier. Its acceptance is at most $T\varepsilon$ if all verifiers accept rarely, and at least $1-2m/2^T-T\varepsilon-\varepsilon$ when a dominant candidate verifies reliably. The extra final $\varepsilon$ is verifier error; the output is an acceptance bit, not a candidate list.
QuarticQuery.Upper.tval: `tval a v f n L` combines candidate generation with eventual sequential verification. With no stages left it equals `vall v L`. Otherwise the process stops with probability $f(L)$ and verifies the current list, or chooses a pivot with normalized weight and continues. The definition has one algebraic recurrence. At total weight zero it equals immediate verification only after the separate premise $f(L)=1$ is supplied.
QuarticQuery.Upper.tval_le: With $n$ stages still available, acceptance is at most $(|L|+n)\varepsilon$ when every verifier accepts with probability at most $\varepsilon$. `ha` bounds comparison entries in $[0,1]$, `hv` bounds verifier probabilities, `hf` bounds stopping probabilities, and `hε0` makes the error nonnegative. No dominant candidate or independence between history-dependent stopping probabilities is assumed. The proof only uses the recursion and its nonnegative weights.
QuarticQuery.Upper.tval_lower: The lower bound is $(1-\varepsilon)(1-I_n(L)-n\varepsilon)$. Besides probability bounds `ha`, `hv`, and `hf`, it requires `hd` for dominance, `hvs` for verifier success at least $1-\varepsilon$, and `hz` for certain stopping when total weight vanishes. `hT` requires $T_0\varepsilon<1/2$; `hfail` bounds stopping only for histories of length at most $T_0$ that miss $s$; `hL` requires $|L|+n\leq T_0$.
QuarticQuery.Upper.uniformOpaqueAmplifie: For a fixed basis origin `o`, Boolean success predicate `S`, and positive parameters with `η < 1/2`, one choice unitary `V` works for every preparation unitary `U`. The successful enlarged state factors as `retainedProduct ξ A.goodState`: auxiliary records times the original successful register. The theorem also bounds failure, gives success at least $p/2$ when $p>0$, and counts logical reads for any `IsCirc n F`. It treats success predicates on basis labels, rather than an arbitrary supplied projector.
QuarticQuery.Upper.vall: `vall v L` is the probability that at least one candidate in the list $L$ accepts when fresh verifiers are run in order. The empty list rejects. For a head $c$, either its verifier accepts with probability $v(c)$, or it rejects and verification continues on the tail. Repeated entries count as repeated fresh attempts. The definition is algebraic; bounds on the probabilities are supplied by subsequent theorems.
QuarticQuery.Upper.vall_le: If each fresh verifier accepts with probability at most $\varepsilon$, the probability that any verification in $L$ accepts is at most $|L|\varepsilon$. `h` supplies the probability bounds and `hε` supplies the common error bound. The list length counts repeated entries. This union bound is used on zero-inputs, where every proposed winning candidate should be rejected.
QuarticQuery.aQueries: The number $N_i$ counts every query to one of column $i$’s auxiliary strings along a specified query list. It adds queries across all $r$ strings, and repeated calls count again. It excludes $X$ bits and certificate-cell bits. Thus $N_i\le L$ implies a separate cap of $L$ on each target string in that column. The definition accepts any list; the paper applies it to the complete dummy execution.
QuarticQuery.address_guess_average: With one-input success bounded by $2/3$, a finite mixture of predictors that each use at most $L$ queries per input guesses all $r$ address bits with weight at most $(2/3)^r$. The hypotheses `hard` and `hT` give the one-input bound and the separate caps. The seed weights `p` have mass one and are independent of the target tuple. The address bits need not themselves be unbiased; the result concerns computing their values from their input strings.
QuarticQuery.addressedF_eq_true_iff: The board's Boolean answer is one exactly when some column and some cell address satisfy the winning conditions. Every complete board has an answer; an unpromised auxiliary input merely prevents its column from winning. The existential search in this statement defines the function and is not a proposed query algorithm. Later upper bounds show how to evaluate it efficiently.
QuarticQuery.addressedF_not_RLe: No randomized program computes the addressed total function within $G$ queries when the three-term discrepancy is below $1/3$. The hypotheses `hL` and `hL1` say that the partial function defeats budget $L\ge1$; `hC` supplies a circuit realizing it. Correctness would force acceptance at most $1/3$ on dummy inputs and at least $2/3$ on supported planted inputs. Their gap contradicts `hdisc`, after averaging the deterministic-tree bounds.
QuarticQuery.alphaTot: The infimum of the nonnegative powers $\alpha$ for which one constant bounds every total Boolean function by $R(f)\le C(1+Q(f))^\alpha$. Expanding `UniversalPower` shows the order: choose $C>0$ before the input length and the function. `sInf` denotes an infimum, not a maximum separation witnessed by one finite function. The later theorem identifies this infimum as four.
QuarticQuery.alphaTot_eq_four_unconditio: The optimal exponent $\alpha_{\mathrm{tot}}$ equals four. This declaration has no remaining `BansalSinhaLower` hypothesis: its proof supplies the established fixed-parameter Forrelation bound to the earlier conditional theorem. The conclusion concerns a universal power with an arbitrary absolute multiplicative constant. It does not assert that a particular finite input achieves $R=Q^4$, or that every printed intermediate argument is the proof used here.
QuarticQuery.avg_foundZero_le: For a fixed column, uniformly averaging the independent zero rows bounds its discovery probability by $2/m$ times its expected number of $X_i$ queries. The auxiliary strings are fixed parameters `A`; they are not conditioned on a search event. Other zero locations are averaged along with the target column’s location. This is the per-column estimate before summing columns, averaging the auxiliary strings, or replacing the total $X$ query count by the tree’s depth.
QuarticQuery.avg_heavy_le: For any query list of length at most $G$, an independent uniformly selected column is heavy with probability at most $G/(mL)$. The hypothesis `hL : 1 ≤ L` permits division by $L$; `hl` bounds the list length. Each auxiliary query belongs to only one column, so their column counts sum to at most the total number of queries. This estimate holds after fixing the dummy run and is then averaged over that run.
QuarticQuery.budgetValue: The value $W_c(\nu)$ is defined recursively. With no queries left it chooses the better constant answer. With one more query it may keep the old value, or query any coordinate and add the two restricted values. The `none` option represents retaining the smaller-budget strategy and makes the recursion meaningful even when there are no coordinates. Off-promise inputs never contribute to success, because their partial-function value is `none`.
QuarticQuery.budgetValue_add_le: The sum of the two restricted values with allowance $c$ is at most the original value with allowance $c+1$. Querying coordinate `q` first and then following either optimal continuation is one permitted strategy in the recursion. The result includes zero-weight and repeated-query branches without a conditional-probability convention. It is the one-input inequality that absorbs the changed factor in the direct-product induction.
QuarticQuery.budgetValue_le_of_forall: If every one-input tree of depth at most $c$ has success weight at most $\beta$, then $W_c(\nu)\le\beta$. The hypothesis `h` is the universal bound on those trees. The proof uses an attaining tree, so the conclusion follows for the recursively defined optimum rather than being assumed as its meaning. At the root of the direct-product argument, this turns the hard-law premise into one factor bounded by $\beta$.
QuarticQuery.budgetValue_nonneg: The optimal weighted success $W_c(\nu)$ is nonnegative whenever every input weight is nonnegative. The premise `hν` states this pointwise condition. A constant answer already has nonnegative success weight, and the optimum is at least that value. This fact allows multiplication of inequalities by the other inputs’ continuation values in the product proof. It does not require total mass one or support on the promise.
QuarticQuery.circuitEval: The true Boolean value of each non-input gate, computed recursively from the actual input and strictly earlier gate values. The gate index decreases in recursive calls, expressing the circuit's topological order. As a function on all gate indices, `circuitEval C x` is the entire transcript. This evaluation is defined even when the input has no promised partial-function value.
QuarticQuery.constantOnPromise_of_isEmpt: If the coordinate type is empty, every partial Boolean function is constant on its promise. There is only one bit input, and it is either undefined or has one Boolean label. Thus the constant-answer alternative of `QLe` supplies the expected zero-query algorithm even though the indexed quantum state space has no unit vector. The theorem includes the empty promise without requiring a distinguished input label.
QuarticQuery.coupledAvg: The joint average first draws every auxiliary input independently with weights $\mu$, then every zero row independently and uniformly, then the selected column independently and uniformly. The three nested averages make the independence of $I$ from the entire dummy run explicit. For a probability interpretation, $\mu$ must have nonnegative weights summing to one. The definition itself accepts arbitrary real weights, so those conditions appear in the theorems using it.
QuarticQuery.cubic_bound_fails_unconditi: No real constant $C$ makes $R(f)\le C Q(f)^3$ hold for every total Boolean function on every nonempty finite cube. The quantifiers range over all $n\ge1$ and all such $f$. This declaration has no Forrelation-hardness hypothesis: it invokes the supplied unconditional lower-bound development. It is the unshifted cubic claim stated in the paper, not merely the version with $1+Q$ in place of $Q$.
QuarticQuery.direct_product_realized_cap: A finite independent choice of possibly uncapped trees has all-correct-and-compliant weight at most $\beta^r$. The one-input premise `hard` bounds depth-$L$ success, and the seed weights `p` form a probability law. Compliance is expressed recursively along the original actual execution. The seed has `[Fintype S]`; the statement does not cover an arbitrary measurable seed. Nor does it directly state compliance as inequalities for the terminal numerical query counts.
QuarticQuery.dummy: The dummy board has $X_i[j]=0$ exactly when $j=J_i$, keeps every supplied auxiliary input $A_{i,h}$, and sets all certificate-cell bits to zero. This definition takes the zero rows and auxiliary inputs as data; it does not draw them randomly. Their independent laws are specified by the averaging definitions. In the three cases of the code, the first case reads an $X$ bit, the second an auxiliary-input bit, and the last a cell bit.
QuarticQuery.eq_of_dummy_ne_planted: If one input bit differs between the dummy and planted boards, its coordinate is either the erased zero $X_I[J_I]$ or a bit of the cell $B_{I,s_I}$. The premise `h` is an actual disagreement of that bit. The conclusion is a necessary condition, not a claim that every bit of the filled cell changes. Some certificate bits may already equal their blank value. The result holds for any supplied transcript data.
QuarticQuery.eval_simTree: If the original run proposes a coordinate naming output $s$ at time `t`, and has used at most `c` target queries before then, the capped simulator outputs $s$. The assumptions `hbase` and `hV` say that outside and target answers agree with the original input. The cap concerns the prefix before the selected query, not its answer. This is the pointwise event inclusion behind the prediction bound; the simulator may also succeed on its default output.
QuarticQuery.existsUnique_gateConsistent: Every input has one and only one gate-consistent transcript: the circuit's evaluated gate values. The existential-uniqueness notation `∃!` asserts both existence and uniqueness. This is independent of whether the input lies in the Forrelation promise. A correct computation on an unpromised input still exists; its domain output is what prevents that transcript from certifying a winner.
QuarticQuery.exists_failing_localTest: A column that wins at no address has at least one failing local test at every proposed address. `hn : ¬ ∃ s, WinsAt …` rules out winning anywhere, while `hC` supplies circuit correctness. The conclusion includes columns with unpromised auxiliary inputs. It does not identify which test fails or give an algorithm for locating that test; quantum search supplies that operation later.
QuarticQuery.exists_fixedSequence: Given `hT : A.queryCap ≤ T`, the theorem produces one enlarged finite workspace, entry isometry, sequence of fixed gates, and accepting projector. For every input and every starting vector, exactly $T$ controlled phase queries reproduce the adaptive program’s true-output mass. The choices precede the input quantifier. The conclusion is a mass identity, not equality of final states or preservation of a designated reusable subsystem.
QuarticQuery.exists_gate: For two isometries `c` and `L` into the same finite query space, there is an input-independent isometry `Z` satisfying $Z(c\phi)=L\phi$ for every source vector. In finite equal dimensions this target isometry is unitary. The proof extends the induced isometry between the embedded subspaces. The result is general linear algebra: compatibility with an oracle comes from the particular embeddings chosen in the query-simulation step.
QuarticQuery.exists_hard_distribution: If no randomized algorithm computes $P$ within $L$ queries, one probability law on promised inputs makes every deterministic depth-$L$ tree succeed with probability at most $2/3$. The premise `h : ¬ RLe f L` expresses that failure of a randomized budget. The law is chosen once, before the tree, and may depend on $P$ and $L$. The conclusion explicitly gives nonnegative weights, total mass one, and promise support. It does not assert a strict margin below $2/3$.
QuarticQuery.exists_nat_exponent: For every real $\alpha<4$, some integer $k\ge2$ satisfies $\alpha/2<2-1/k$. This is the parameter choice that leaves a positive power of $m$ in the quotient. The only premise is `hα : α < 4`; nonnegativity of $\alpha$ is not needed for choosing $k$. The theorem gives existence of a suitable integer rather than prescribing the paper’s particular sufficient inequality $k>2/(4-\alpha)$.
QuarticQuery.exists_tree_budgetValue_le: There exists a tree of depth at most $c$ whose weighted success is at least $W_c(\nu)$. Together with the companion upper bound for every such tree, this proves that the recursive value is an attained maximum. The statement itself supplies the attaining direction, not both inequalities. Its proof chooses an optimal constant at depth zero and an optimal recursion option at the next depth. No normalized probability law is required.
QuarticQuery.finite_depth_le: On a finite coordinate set, the set of deterministic Boolean-output trees with depth at most $n$ is finite. At depth zero there are two leaves; at higher depth one chooses a coordinate and two smaller trees, or stops. This supports both the finite maximum in the continuation value and the finite payoff matrix in minimax. It counts syntactic trees, including redundant queries and branches with inconsistent repeated answers.
QuarticQuery.forrelationDenominator: The integer denominator is $2^{2t}(2^t)^{k-1}=m(\sqrt m)^{k-1}$ for $m=4^t$. Keeping it integral allows the promise thresholds to be tested by exact integer comparisons. It supplies the normalization of the whole unnormalized path sum. Equivalently, each of its $k-1$ Walsh factors can be normalized separately, leaving an overall factor $1/m$.
QuarticQuery.forrelationNumerator: The numerator sums one sign monomial for every path choosing a coordinate in each block. Every summand also contains the unnormalized Walsh signs between consecutive blocks. Lean uses integer arithmetic throughout this definition. Dividing by $m(\sqrt m)^{k-1}$ gives the real statistic $\Phi$, so moving each normalization factor into its Walsh entry yields the paper’s $1/m$ path expansion.
QuarticQuery.forrelation_lower_uniform_s: For $k\ge2$ and $15k+2\le2t$, the randomized query complexity exceeds $\frac{2}{18225}\frac{m^{1-1/k}}{k^2\ln(4km)}$, where $m=4^t$. The binders `hk` and `ht` state these two conditions. The constant and logarithm are explicit, so the bound can be used when $k$ varies with $t$. The conclusion concerns the promise problem $P$, before the addressed total function is constructed.
QuarticQuery.four_mul_sq_le_two_pow: For every natural number $t\ge8$, $4t^2\le2^t$. The premise `ht` gives the exact starting threshold. The proof checks the base case and uses the fact that the square grows by at most a factor two at each later step. This is the arithmetic input that makes the query allowance at least one uniformly for every integer $k\ge2$. It is independent of query algorithms or hardness.
QuarticQuery.gateConsistent_iff_eq_circu: A proposed transcript passes every gate equation if and only if it equals the circuit's true evaluation. No promise or circuit-correctness hypothesis is required: this holds for any acyclic circuit and every raw input. The forward direction uses induction through earlier gates. This explains why checking small local equations can certify a long computation without recomputing it in full.
QuarticQuery.guessSuccess_le_prod: For independent input weights $\nu_h$ and a tree with allowance $c_h$ on every branch, the weight of getting all answers right is at most $\prod_h W_{c_h}(\nu_h)$. The premise `hν` requires nonnegative weights and `hT` requires separate caps. The weights may have different masses and need not share one law. The proof works before normalization, so it includes impossible branches without conditional distributions.
QuarticQuery.guessSuccess_leaf: At a leaf, the tree outputs a fixed Boolean vector $s$. Its all-correct weight under independent input weights is exactly the product of the one-input constant-answer weights. This equality is the base case of the weighted induction and the equality behind the terminal conditional calculation after normalization. It requires no cap or hardness assumption. It is an average over the independent tuple, not a pointwise bound on a successful tuple.
QuarticQuery.hadamard_phaseOracle_hadama: Applying a Hadamard to the answer bit, then the controlled phase oracle, then another Hadamard gives exactly the bit-oracle action on every state vector. The phase oracle keeps the answer bit as a control, so it can act trivially when that bit is zero. This is an equality of states using one oracle call, not merely an equality of outcome probabilities. A bare uncontrolled phase oracle is a different interface.
QuarticQuery.localTest: The Boolean test selected by its label at candidate $(i,s)$. Its cases inspect a column bit, a pointer's target bit, one gate equation, the domain output, or the value output. In the last two cases `false` labels the domain test and `true` labels the value test; these are labels, not expected outcomes. Every test returns a Boolean on every board.
QuarticQuery.localTests_iff_eq_of_winsAt: If column $i$ wins at $s$, then all local tests at another address $s'$ pass exactly when $s'=s$. Both the winning hypothesis `hw` and circuit correctness `hC` are required. This addresses a false proposed address even when its pointers and gate values look plausible: at least one test must fail unless the address agrees with the defined auxiliary answers.
QuarticQuery.log_four_k_m_le: If $1\le k\le t$ and $m=4^t$, then $\ln(4km)\le6t$. The binders `hk` and `hkt` state the range. Lean uses $\ln(4k)\le4k-1$ and $\ln2\le1$. This estimate converts the uniform lower bound into a sufficient threshold for the fixed-$k$ floor allowance; it does not choose that threshold itself.
QuarticQuery.lvalue_lt_R_explicit: For $k\ge2$ and $t\ge3499200k^2$, the integer allowance $L_{k,4^t}$ is strictly smaller than $R(P_{k,4^t})$. Those conditions are the binders `hk` and `ht`. This declaration uses the older, coarser uniform constant. The paper derives the smaller threshold $13669k^2$ from the sharp uniform bound; that smaller threshold is not the hypothesis of this named theorem.
QuarticQuery.norm_sq_eq_project_add: For a basis subset $S$ and any vector $\psi$, the squared norm is the sum of the squared norms of `project S ψ` and its complementary component. The vector need not be normalized, and the empty subset and zero vector are included. This orthogonal decomposition justifies adding unnormalized branch masses after a measurement. It is not a theorem about arbitrary measurement dilation or mixed-state purification.
QuarticQuery.one_le_Lvalue: For $k\ge2$ and $t\ge8$, the floored allowance $L$ is at least one. The premises `hk` and `ht` are uniform thresholds in the construction. The proof compares the numerator’s exponent with $1/2$, then uses $4t^2\le2^t$ to show that the unfloored ratio is at least one. This establishes the lower end of the range needed by the planted lower-bound theorem.
QuarticQuery.planted: The planted board turns column $I$ into all ones and fills only its cell at the true address. The filled cell stores the supplied transcripts and pointers to the other columns’ zero rows. Every auxiliary-input bit stays unchanged. The argument `tr` supplies transcripts; validity is not part of this definition and is required later by the theorem that the planted board has value one. Outside the selected column and cell, the board remains the dummy board.
QuarticQuery.reindex: For a coordinate bijection `e : ι ≃ κ`, the renamed function on a $\kappa$-input evaluates the original function at `fun i => x (e i)`. Values and promise membership are transported together. The operation changes names only; it does not add input information or an oracle call. The separate reindexing theorems establish invariance of the three complexity measures.
QuarticQuery.restrictWeight: The restricted weight keeps $\nu(x)$ when the queried coordinate has answer $b$, and assigns weight zero otherwise. It does not divide by the probability of that answer. Thus it records both the remaining possibilities and their original mass. A repeated consistent answer leaves this weight unchanged; an inconsistent answer gives zero everywhere. The definition makes sense for arbitrary weights, while probability and product inequalities later assume nonnegativity.
QuarticQuery.totalise: `totalise f` returns `some (f x)` on every input. It changes the representation of a total Boolean function without restricting its domain or changing its value. This lets the same definitions of $D$, $R$, and $Q$ handle total functions and promise problems. The repeated appearance of `totalise` in the quartic bound therefore imposes correctness on every bit string.
QuarticQuery.treeSuccess_le_budgetValue: Every tree with `hT : T.depth ≤ c` has weighted success at most $W_c(\nu)$. Splitting on the first query gives two restricted weights; the recursive maximum includes the sum of the corresponding smaller-budget values. This is the upper-bound half of the identification of $W_c$ with optimal weighted success. The other half constructs an attaining tree. The statement permits unnormalized weights and counts repeated queries toward depth.
QuarticQuery.trueAddress: The true address of column $i$ is the $r$-bit vector of its auxiliary answers. The required argument `hdef : ∀ h, promised f (readA x i h)` says that every auxiliary input in that column is promised. No promise is required in other columns. A column with one undefined auxiliary answer has no true address in this sense, although the decoder can still return an arbitrary bit string.
QuarticQuery.winner_finds_zero: The pointer stored in a winning cell finds a zero in every other column. The hypothesis `h : WinsAt … i s` fixes the correct winning address, and `hne : j ≠ i` chooses a rival. Together with the incoming-pointer fact, this shows that correct decoding of the winner alone is enough for it to win a comparison.
QuarticQuery.winner_no_incoming_zero: If column $i$ wins, every pointer into it from a distinct column reaches a one, whatever cell address that other column uses. The only substantive hypothesis is the winning condition `h`; `hne` makes the source and target distinct. No promise or successful decoding is assumed in the other column. This is the deterministic reason a genuine winner cannot be disqualified.
QuarticQuery.winsAt_iff_localTests: The candidate $(i,s)$ wins if and only if every local test passes. The hypothesis `hC : CircuitRealises C f` supplies the meaning of the circuit's two outputs. Gate consistency identifies the true transcript, the domain test excludes unpromised inputs, and the value test pins the proposed address. The equivalence holds on every complete board, including malformed certificates.
QuarticQuery.winsAt_unique: Two winning pairs on the same board must have both the same column and the same address. The hypotheses `h` and `h'` assert that each pair wins. Different winning columns would contradict the first winner's pointer to a zero in the second all-one column. Within one column, the auxiliary answers determine the address uniquely. Circuit correctness is unnecessary for this argument.
QuarticQuery.xQueries: The query cost $Q_i$ counts every occurrence of an $X_i$ coordinate along the complete dummy run. Repeated queries and queries after the zero is found are included. Queries to auxiliary inputs and certificate cells do not count toward this particular quantity. Lean writes the count as a real number because the next step averages it over zero locations. This cost is deliberately different from the one-per-column discovery indicator.
QuarticQuery.zero_search_sum: For every finite set $U$ of possible zero rows, $|U|$ times the number of worlds where the zero is queried is at most twice the summed number of column queries. The hypotheses `hout` and `hin` require identical outside answers and exactly one zero at its designated row in each world. Queries after discovery and repeated queries count toward cost. No distribution or worst-case depth bound is needed for this combinatorial inequality.
QuarticQuery.zero_search_sum_successor: Across a finite set $U$ of possible zero locations, $(|U|+1)$ times the number of successful searches is at most twice their total column-query cost. The maps `e` and `c` identify the column; `hout` fixes every outside answer across the worlds and `hin` gives each world its unique zero. Repeats and reads after discovery count toward cost. The statement is the one-column ingredient for the denominator $m+1$, not the averaged two-clause bound in the paper.
